title: The whirlwind
hookLine: a whirlwind doesn't last all morning; speak little (Tao Te Ching 23)

cards: The sky goes green-gray in the middle of the afternoon. Wind tears through the street, a trash can rolls past on its side, rain comes down so hard it bounces. Everyone ducks into doorways.
And then, almost before the shirts are soaked, it's over. The sun is out, and someone is already wiping off a café chair. While a storm like that is happening, it can seem as if it will never stop.
It does. Chapter twenty-three of the Tao Te Ching watches one blow through, and draws a lesson about how much we say.

teach.b: First, speak little, like nature. The chapter opens with just a few characters that link saying little with what is so of itself, the natural way of things. Nature doesn't talk much.
Second, no storm lasts all morning. In Legge's translation: "A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day." Who makes the wind and the rain?

Heaven and earth, the chapter says. And if even heaven and earth can't keep up a burst like that for long, how much less can a person. A rant, a lecture, a flood of messages late at night: loud and fast runs out.
Third, you become what you follow. Whoever follows the Way becomes one with the Way. Whoever follows virtue becomes one with virtue.
And whoever follows loss becomes one with loss. What you keep company with, you turn into, and the Way, it adds, is glad to have you.

teach.h: A VIOLENT WIND DOES NOT LAST.
teach.b: The chapter closes with a line the book used before, in chapter seventeen: where trust falls short, there is no trust in return. Too many words can be a sign of that.
People who trust each other don't need to keep talking.
And this closes a week: leaders whose people said we did it ourselves, the way lost, the uncarved block, drifting like an infant, the elusive and real, yielding to be whole, and now the whirlwind.

how: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty-three as a practice of restraint in speech: saying what is needed, then stopping, and letting strong feelings pass before they talk.

games.q: you're in the middle of a whirlwind of a conversation, loud and fast. what does chapter twenty-three suggest?
o: say little, and let the storm blow itself out.
keep sending messages so nothing is left unsaid.
games.why: a violent wind doesn't last a whole morning. the chapter opens with saying little, the natural way of things.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you need to say to someone: a request, an answer, an apology, a no. Say it silently the long way, with every reason and softener, then again in half the words, then once more with only what's needed.
Sit in the quiet after that last, plain version, and let it be enough.

wordCard.voice: The whirlwind. Chapter twenty-three's violent wind that can't last a whole morning, and its advice to say little, the way nature does. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, xī yán zìrán: few words, what is so of itself. The opening of Tao Te Ching 23.
